title: CloudPipe deployment inputs
description:
Every cluster-wide value a human supplies to stand up a CloudPipe deployment, and nothing else. `pixi run cloudpipe setup` reads this file rather than hard-coding its questions, and renders `terraform.tfvars` and `backend.tf` into a target Terraform root from the answers.

This is the integration contract for any front end. A caller reads it and renders a complete input form without opening another file: `title` is the prompt, `description` is the help text, `pattern` is the rule, `x-section` is the grouping, and `x-source` says where a human obtains the value. Fields marked `x-derived` are computed and overridable — a form generator must display the computed value and accept a change, but must NOT present them as questions.

The eight Globus variables are deliberately absent. `pixi run globus init` owns them and renders them into a separate `globus.auto.tfvars`; see `src/globus_admin/schemas/answers.schema.json`. The two sets are disjoint and a test holds them so, because two tools writing one variable is two tools disagreeing about it.

There is deliberately NO AWS credential, key, or profile field, and no Cloudflare API token field. AWS credentials come from the deployer's environment through an AWS CLI v2 SSO profile; the Cloudflare token comes from CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN. Neither is ever prompted for, stored, or printed.

Every `pattern` here is the mechanical equivalent of a `validation` block in `terraform/modules/stack/variables.tf`, and `tests/test_setup_wizard_schema.py` derives both sides from that file and asserts they agree. A field whose variable Terraform does not constrain carries no pattern: one invented here would reject values Terraform accepts, which is the single failure a deployer cannot work around. `x-error-message` is Terraform's own `error_message`, verbatim, so the two can never word the same rule differently.

No value in this file identifies any deployment. Where a shape needs illustrating, the description uses a placeholder or a reserved example name.

x-required-when.state_bucket: The backend block is being rendered, which is the default. `cloudpipe setup --no-backend` skips both the file and this requirement.

region.x-error-message: region must be an AWS region id: two letters, a dash, a word, a dash, a digit.
region.title: AWS region
region.description:
The AWS region to run in, for example eu-west-1 (Ireland) or ap-southeast-2 (Sydney). Choose the region where your imaging data is stored, or the one closest to you.

Keeping the data and the processing in one region avoids transfer charges and delays. Not every region offers the GPU machines the pipeline uses, so check that yours does before you choose. All regions are listed at https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-infrastructure/latest/regions/aws-regions.html.

name.x-error-message: name must be 3 to 20 characters: lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter and not ending in a hyphen.
name.title: Short name for this deployment
name.description:
A short name that labels everything the install creates in your AWS account: 3 to 20 lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter. The default is fine unless one AWS account will hold more than one deployment.

Storage bucket names also get a random six-character code after this name, generated for you, because bucket names must be unique across all of AWS.

Avoid the words aws, amazon and cognito anywhere in it: the sign-in page's web address starts with this name, and AWS refuses addresses that contain them.

bucket_suffix.x-error-message: bucket_suffix must be empty or exactly 6 lowercase letters and digits.
bucket_suffix.title: Random code in storage bucket names
bucket_suffix.description:
A random six-character code added to every storage bucket name. It is generated once and kept, so there is nothing to do.

Bucket names are global across all AWS accounts. Without the code, two deployments with the same name would collide, and anyone could claim a predictable name before you. It is kept in the answers file, so every re-run and every computer you resume on uses the same buckets. Change it only before the buckets are created (Step 4 of the deployer guide); afterwards a new code names buckets that do not exist.

domain.x-error-message: domain must be null (port-forward mode) or a bare DNS name with a TLD, e.g. example.org — no scheme and no trailing dot.
domain.x-null-meaning: port-forward mode: no published web UIs, and no domain or hosted zone needed
domain.title: Web address for the dashboards (or none)
domain.description:
Type none unless you own a domain name that is set up in this AWS account (Route 53) and want the web dashboards at addresses like grafana.<your domain>. With none, you open each dashboard from your own computer with one command instead, which is the simpler choice.

With a domain: a Route 53 hosted zone for exactly that name must already exist in the account you are deploying into, and the domain's registrar must point at it, because the install proves you own the domain through it to get web certificates. Type the bare name, for example lab.example.org, with no https:// and no trailing dot. `cloudpipe preflight` checks that the zone exists.

With none, nothing is published at any address. You open a dashboard with `pixi run --manifest-path <your clone>/pixi.toml cloudpipe ui <name>`, while connected to WARP.

items.x-error-message: operator_emails must be email addresses with a lower-case domain, e.g. operator@example.org.

operator_emails.x-error-message: operator_emails must hold at least one address: with none, no one can administer the deployment.
operator_emails.title: Email addresses of the people who will run it
operator_emails.description:
The email address of each person who will operate this deployment, separated by commas, for example ana@example.edu, ben@example.edu. These people can sign in, connect to the cluster and administer the web dashboards.

Each person gets a sign-in account with a password and an authenticator app (such as Google Authenticator or 1Password) as a second step. The install creates the sign-in system but not the accounts themselves: when it gets there, the installer prints the command to run for each person, and Step 8 of docs/deployer-first-hour.md explains it. The dashboards admit only the email domains listed here.

cognito_federation.title: Your institution's single sign-on (optional)
cognito_federation.description:
Lets operators sign in with your institution's own single sign-on instead of a separate password. Leave it out unless you need it: sign-in works fully without it.

This is the one setting the wizard does not ask for, because its details belong to your institution and arranging it takes a conversation with their identity team. Write it into the answers file by hand; `cloudpipe setup` uses it and `cloudpipe preflight` checks it. See docs/deployer-first-hour.md, "Signing in with your institution's identity provider".

`type` is "saml" (with `metadata_url`) or "oidc" (with `oidc_issuer` and `client_secret_id`, the name of a Secrets Manager secret you create by hand holding {"clientID": ..., "clientSecret": ...}).

`mfa_evidence` is required and takes exactly one form, because Cognito adds no second factor of its own for a federated user: either `claim` and `claim_value`, a per-login claim the Cloudflare Access policy will then require, or `attestation`, a reference to their written policy for a provider that cannot assert one.
cognito_federation.x-not-asked: Its shape is the institution's, and a nested object is not a question a line-oriented prompt can ask well. Write it in the answers document; it is validated and rendered like every other field.
cognito_federation.x-null-meaning: no institutional provider: operators sign in to the Cognito pool itself

name.x-error-message: cognito_federation.name must be 2 to 32 printable characters and may not begin or end with an underscore or a space.

metadata_url.x-error-message: cognito_federation.metadata_url is required for a SAML provider and must be an https URL.

allOf.x-error-message: cognito_federation.oidc_issuer is required for an OIDC provider and must be an https URL.
cognito_federation.oidc_issuer must not end in a slash — Cognito appends the discovery path to it.

client_secret_id.x-error-message: cognito_federation.client_secret_id is required for an OIDC provider: the name of a hand-created Secrets Manager secret holding {"clientID": ..., "clientSecret": ...}.

attribute_mapping.x-error-message: cognito_federation.attribute_mapping must map `email`: every web UI signs in on the email address, and an unmapped one leaves the federated user with no identity the deployment can match.

mfa_evidence.x-error-message: cognito_federation.mfa_evidence must declare exactly one form: either `claim` AND `claim_value` (a per-login claim the Access policy will require), or `attestation` (a reference to the institution's written MFA policy). Cognito delegates authentication to the provider and adds no second factor of its own, so one of the two is what satisfies NIST 800-171 3.5.3.

github_repo.x-error-message: github_repo must be in owner/repo format, with no scheme and no .git suffix.
github_repo.title: GitHub repository allowed to build images (owner/name)
github_repo.description:
The GitHub repository allowed to build and upload container images for this deployment, written as owner/name, for example your-lab/cloudpipe. Give your own fork of CloudPipe, even if you never build images: the install needs a repository here, and nothing breaks if it never builds.

Give a repository you control, not someone else's: GitHub Actions runs on its main branch can upload images into your AWS account. Type it without https:// and without .git.

This does not have to be the repository the cluster follows, which is the next question. They are usually the same.

gitops_repo_url.x-error-message: gitops_repo_url must be an https clone URL — ArgoCD reads it without a credential here.
gitops_repo_url.title: Repository the cluster follows (its web address)
gitops_repo_url.description:
The https address of the repository the cluster takes its configuration from, for example https://github.com/your-lab/cloudpipe. Usually your fork of CloudPipe. The cluster keeps itself in step with this repository, so changes merged there are applied automatically.

It must be an https address, not an ssh one (git@...). A public repository needs no password; for a private one, see docs/deployer-first-hour.md, "If your GitOps repository is private".

github_user_url.x-error-message: github_user_url must be an https URL.
github_user_url.title: GitHub account or organization that owns it
github_user_url.description:
The https address of the GitHub user or organization that owns the repository above, for example https://github.com/your-lab.

Used so that one access setting covers every repository under that owner, rather than one per repository.

github_oidc_allowed_subs.x-error-message: github_oidc_allowed_subs must not be empty: an empty list trusts nothing and every build loses its credentials.
github_oidc_allowed_subs.title: Which GitHub Actions runs may build images
github_oidc_allowed_subs.description:
Which GitHub Actions runs may use the image-building permissions: runs on the main branch of the repository you gave. Worked out for you, so there is nothing to do.

These are the exact `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` claim values allowed to assume the GitHub Actions roles. Override it when you need one of three things, all of which the stack's own variable documents: a non-main branch, temporarily, to test a build workflow before merging it; a job that sets a GitHub `environment:`, which mints repo:<repo>:environment:<name> and would NOT match a ref-shaped entry; or a wildcard, since the trust policy uses StringLike and `*` is a wildcard in these values.

An entry that matches nothing is not an error anywhere: the job simply loses its credentials. That is why this is worked out rather than typed.

cloudflare_account_id.x-error-message: cloudflare_account_id must be the 32-character hex account id from the Cloudflare dashboard.
cloudflare_account_id.title: Cloudflare account ID
cloudflare_account_id.description:
The 32-character ID of the Cloudflare account to use (digits and the letters a to f), not your login email. In the Cloudflare dashboard, press Cmd/Ctrl+K, type 'Copy account ID' and choose it: the ID is copied to your clipboard.

Use a Cloudflare account for this deployment alone. Several of its settings exist once per account, so two deployments sharing one would overwrite each other. The ID is also shown under Workers & Pages > Account Details. If your API token is already exported, `curl -s https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN"` lists the accounts it can reach, which also confirms it is the right one.

cloudflare_team_domain.title: Cloudflare Zero Trust team address
cloudflare_team_domain.description:
Your Zero Trust team name followed by .cloudflareaccess.com, for example my-lab.cloudflareaccess.com. You chose the team name when you turned on Zero Trust in the Cloudflare dashboard; it is shown under Zero Trust > Settings.

If Zero Trust is not on yet: open Zero Trust from the account's sidebar, choose a team name, then the Free plan. Cloudflare asks for payment details even for Free, and charges nothing. Only the dashboard can do this step; the install cannot do it for you.

Everyone's sign-in goes through this address, so it appears in every link WARP and the browser use. docs/deployer-first-hour.md, "The Cloudflare account and its token", covers the same step.

cloudflare_team_name.title: A display name for your Zero Trust team
cloudflare_team_name.description:
Any readable label, for example your lab's name. There is nothing to look up.

The install sets it on your Zero Trust organization, replacing the placeholder name Cloudflare created when Zero Trust was turned on. That placeholder can look like a web address, but it is not the team address of the previous question.

state_bucket.x-error-message: state_bucket must be a valid S3 bucket name.
state_bucket.title: Storage bucket for the install's records
state_bucket.description:
The storage bucket where the install keeps its record of what it has built (Terraform's "state"). It is named for you, <name>-<code>-terraform-state, so there is nothing to do. The bucket itself is created in Step 4 of the deployer guide.

Override it only to use a state bucket you already have, and then also set terraform_state_bucket to the same name in a `.auto.tfvars` file, or the audit trail watches a bucket that does not exist. Use a bucket kept for this purpose alone, not the data bucket. `cloudpipe setup --no-backend` skips this entirely if you keep the record another way.

state_key.title: Name of the record inside that bucket
state_key.description:
Press Enter to keep the default. Change it only if one bucket will hold the records of more than one deployment.

Two deployments using the same name here would overwrite each other's record.

freesurfer_license_path.title: Your FreeSurfer license file
freesurfer_license_path.description:
The full path to the license.txt file FreeSurfer emailed you, for example /home/you/license.txt. Registration is free at https://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/registration.html. Press Enter to skip it and upload the file yourself later.

The brain-segmentation steps need it, and licenses are issued per person, so CloudPipe cannot ship one. The wizard checks that the file exists and looks like a license, but never copies its contents into your answers or prints them. The bootstrap step (Step 4 of the deployer guide) uploads it to your data bucket.
freesurfer_license_path.x-null-meaning: you upload the license yourself, to config/fslicense in the data bucket; preflight's aws.config_objects says whether it is there

section.description: Field groupings, in the order a front end should present them. The identifiers are stable; the titles are display text.

x-order.title: Where the install keeps its records

source.description: Where a human obtains the value. A front end may group or annotate by this; the wizard shows it alongside the help text, because "go and look this up" is a different kind of answer from "decide this".
